twist.stem: The news says prices in March were 5% above a set earlier point. Amit tells his flatmate that prices rose 5% since February. What is the mix-up?
twist.hint: Which earlier date is the figure measured from?

options.text: It compares with last March.
options.feedback: Right. India's inflation rate compares prices with the same month a year earlier, not with last month.

options.text: The 5% counts food prices alone.
options.feedback: The figure covers a wide basket of retail prices, not just food. The mix-up is the date it compares with.

options.text: The base is January of this year.
options.feedback: There is no January start. Each month's prices are compared with the same month a year before.

transfer.stem: A news report says inflation is 5% this year. Prices at Shalu's local market in Ranchi rose 8%. Is the report wrong?
transfer.hint: Where is the data for the report gathered?

options.text: Yes; her market shows the true figure.
options.feedback: One market is a small slice. The report pools prices from markets across India.

options.text: No; it pools prices from all over India.
options.feedback: Right. Staff record prices in markets across India, so one town's market can differ from the all-India figure.

options.text: Yes; inflation should come out the same in each town.
options.feedback: Towns can differ. The figure is a broad measure built from many markets.

twist.stem: Mr Sharma gets a fixed pension of ₹15,000 a month that does not change. Prices rise each year. What happens to his pension?
twist.hint: Think about the same rupees against higher prices.

options.text: It holds its value.
options.feedback: A fixed amount is not fixed buying power. When prices rise, the same cash buys less.

options.text: It grows a bit.
options.feedback: A fixed sum does not grow. With rising prices, it buys less each year.

options.text: It buys a bit less each year.
options.feedback: Right. People on fixed incomes lose buying power when prices rise, as the same rupees cover less.

transfer.stem: Deepak gets a 12% raise at his job in Indore, and prices rose 6%. His friend Mona gets 3%, with the same 6% price rise. Who can buy more than last year?
transfer.hint: Compare each raise with the rise in prices.

options.text: Just Deepak.
options.feedback: Right. Deepak's raise beat prices, so his real income rose. Mona's 3% is below 6%, so hers fell.

options.text: Both, since both got raises.
options.feedback: A raise smaller than the price rise still buys less. Mona's 3% trails the 6% rise.

options.text: Neither, since prices rose for both.
options.feedback: Deepak's 12% is more than the 6% price rise, so he can buy more than before.

twist.stem: Inflation comes in at 1.5% this year. Is that inside the RBI's band?
twist.hint: Picture where the band starts.

options.text: Yes, lower is better.
options.feedback: Lower is not always better. The band has a floor of 2%, because falling prices can make people wait to buy.

options.text: No, it is below the 2% lower limit.
options.feedback: Right. The band runs from 2% to 6%, so 1.5% sits just below it.

options.text: Yes, since anything under 6% is inside.
options.feedback: The band has two edges, 2% and 6%. Below 2% is outside it too.

transfer.stem: A shopkeeper in Varanasi hears inflation is 3.5% and worries that prices are out of control. What is a fair reply?
transfer.hint: Recall the aim and its limits.

options.text: He is right; any rise above zero means trouble.
options.feedback: A little inflation is normal. The target is about 4%, not zero.

options.text: It is far above the 1% target.
options.feedback: The target is about 4%, not 1%. At 3.5%, prices are rising close to the aim.

options.text: That sits inside the 2% to 6% band.
options.feedback: Right. India aims for about 4%, inside a 2% to 6% band, so 3.5% is within it.

twist.stem: ₹6,000 saved at 10% a year, with gains left in, is ₹7,260 after two years. What does year three add?
twist.hint: Work it on the latest total.

options.feedback: Right. Year three earns 10% on ₹7,260, which includes past gains, so it adds ₹726.
₹600 is 10% of the first sum only. With gains left in, the gain is worked on the bigger total.
₹660 was year two's gain. Year three works on ₹7,260, so it adds more.

transfer.stem: A sari shop in Surat puts each year's profit back into stock, and the stock earns at the same rate. Compared with taking the profit out each year, what happens?
transfer.hint: What base is used each year?

options.text: Its yearly gain stays the same.
options.feedback: That fits taking profit out. Left in, past gains earn as well, so the yearly gain grows.

options.text: Its yearly gain gets bigger over time.
options.feedback: Right. Gains left in start earning too, so each year's gain is worked on a bigger base.

options.text: It ends with the same total either way.
options.feedback: Gains left in earn more gains, so ploughing profit back ends with a bigger total.

twist.stem: Saved once at 5% a year, ₹365 is about ₹466 after 5 years and about ₹1,578 after 30. It gains about ₹100 in the first 5 years. About how much does it gain from year 5 to year 30?
twist.hint: Take the later total and subtract the earlier one.

options.text: About ₹500, at ₹100 for each five years.
options.feedback: That treats each five years as equal. Each year's gain is worked on a bigger pot, so later years add more.

options.text: About ₹600.
options.feedback: Check the sum: ₹1,578 minus ₹466 is about ₹1,100. Later years add much more than early ones.

options.text: About ₹1,100.
options.feedback: Right. ₹1,578 minus ₹466 is about ₹1,100. Growth on growth speeds up as the pot gets bigger.

transfer.stem: Rafiq's father has kept one 5% deposit running for 28 years. He plans to break it two years early, thinking the last two years add little. What does the step suggest?
transfer.hint: Think about the size of the base in late years.

options.text: The final stretch adds the most money.
options.feedback: Right. Each year's gain is worked on a bigger pot, so the last years add the most rupees.

options.text: Each year adds about the same, so little is lost.
options.feedback: Years do not add the same. Growth on growth means later years add more than early ones.

options.text: Late years add less.
options.feedback: Growth speeds up, not down, when gains stay in. The late years add the most.

twist.stem: Two friends each put ₹3,000 a month into different funds through SIPs. After a year, one is up and one is down. How can that be?
twist.hint: What does each of them choose when setting it up?

options.text: One of them must have missed payments.
options.feedback: Missed payments are not needed to explain it. Two funds can simply move in different ways.

options.text: SIPs fix what goes in, not what the fund earns.
options.feedback: Right. A SIP sets the sum and the dates. Each fund's investments can rise or fall in value.

options.text: SIPs promise the same return, so one is an error.
options.feedback: A SIP does not set a return. The money goes into investments that can rise or fall.

transfer.stem: A jeweller in Thrissur offers a monthly gold plan: ₹1,000 each month buys gold at that day's price. What does the plan fix?
transfer.hint: Which parts does the buyer choose in advance?

options.text: The gold per payment.
options.feedback: Each payment buys at that day's price, so the amount of gold changes month to month.

options.text: The end value.
options.feedback: The end value depends on gold prices, which rise and fall. The plan fixes only the payments.

options.text: What you pay and when.
options.feedback: Right. Like a SIP, it sets the payment and the dates, while the price of what you buy moves.

twist.stem: You want money to double in about 6 years. Roughly what steady yearly rate would do that?
twist.hint: Turn the sum around: 72 divided by what gives 6?

options.text: About 12%.
options.feedback: Right. 72 divided by 12 is 6, so a steady 12% doubles money in about six years.

options.text: About 6%.
options.feedback: At 6%, the rule gives 72 divided by 6, which is about 12 years, not six.

options.text: About 18%.
options.feedback: At 18%, money doubles in about four years. For six years, the rate is about 12%.

transfer.stem: Ganesh's family plot near Hubli rises in value at a steady 9% a year. Roughly how long until its value doubles?
transfer.hint: Use the shortcut on the yearly rate.

options.text: About 11 years, since 100 ÷ 9 is 11.
options.feedback: The shortcut uses 72, not 100. 72 divided by 9 gives about eight years.

options.text: About 8 years.
options.feedback: Right. 72 divided by 9 is 8, so the value doubles in about eight years at a steady 9%.

options.text: About 9 years, the same as the rate.
options.feedback: The rate and the years are not the same number. Divide 72 by 9 to get about eight.

twist.stem: A ₹6,000 card balance is left unpaid at 18% a year. Roughly what does it grow to after about 12 years?
twist.hint: Count how many doubling spans fit in 12 years.

options.feedback: That is one doubling. At 18% it doubles about every four years, so 12 years means three doublings.
That is two doublings. Twelve years at 18% gives three, so about ₹48,000.
Right. At 18%, debt doubles in about four years. Three doublings turn ₹6,000 into about ₹48,000.

transfer.stem: Raju borrows ₹7,000 from a local lender at 3% a month and repays nothing. About how long until he owes ₹14,000?
transfer.hint: Change the monthly rate to a yearly one first.

options.text: About 2 years.
options.feedback: Right. 3% a month is about 36% a year, and 72 divided by 36 is 2, so it doubles in about two years.

options.text: About 24 years, since 72 ÷ 3 is 24.
options.feedback: The rule needs a yearly rate. 3% a month is about 36% a year, so it doubles in about two.

options.text: It stays ₹7,000 until he starts paying.
options.feedback: Unpaid debt gathers interest too, so it grows even when nothing is paid.

twist.stem: A fund's ad says it averaged 12% over ten years, so "your money doubles every 6 years." What is the catch?
twist.hint: Did the fund grow by the same amount every time?

options.text: None; an average rate works like a fixed one.
options.feedback: An average hides ups and downs. The shortcut needs a steady rate, which market returns lack.

options.text: Real returns swing from year to year.
options.feedback: Right. Market returns have no fixed rate, so the shortcut only says what would happen if the rate held.

options.text: It is for debt, not savings.
options.feedback: It works for both savings and debt at a steady rate. The catch is that fund returns are not steady.

transfer.stem: A mango farmer's income rose 30% one year and fell 20% the next. His son divides 72 by 30 to say income doubles in under 3 years. What is wrong?
transfer.hint: Does the change stay the same from one year to the next?

options.text: He should divide by 20 instead.
options.feedback: Neither year's rate fits, up or down. The shortcut needs a rate that holds still.

options.text: The rule works for any rate, steady or not.
options.feedback: It gives a fair guess only for a steady rate. Swinging income does not fit.

options.text: No single rate fits.
options.feedback: Right. The shortcut needs a steady rate. Income that jumps and falls has no single rate to divide by.

twist.stem: Varun says his fund is risk-free because it has not lost money in three years. What does its risk still include?
twist.hint: Is next year's result known?

options.text: The chance it could fall in future.
options.feedback: Right. Risk includes the chance of loss and uncertain results. Past gains do not remove that.

options.text: Three good years show it can be called safe.
options.feedback: Good years do not make the future sure. A fund can still lose value.

options.text: Just fraud.
options.feedback: Risk is wider than fraud. It covers any chance of loss or an uncertain result.

transfer.stem: Kavita leaves a salaried job to open a bakery in Mangaluru. Her income could end up higher or lower than before. What does risk mean here?
transfer.hint: Can she know ahead how it turns out?

options.text: A sure loss.
options.feedback: Risk is a chance, not a sure loss. Her income could also end up higher.

options.text: Her income is not known in advance.
options.feedback: Right. Risk includes uncertain results and the chance of loss. Her income could rise or fall.

options.text: Just bad luck.
options.feedback: Risk is not luck alone. It covers any result that is not sure, like the income from a new shop.

twist.stem: Why do riskier investments tend to earn more over long spans?
twist.hint: What would make a rough ride worth it?

options.text: Risky firms are usually better run.
options.feedback: Risk is about swings, not good management. The extra return pays for the extra risk.

options.text: Higher risk means a sure higher gain.
options.feedback: The gain is not sure. A high possible return can come with a loss too.

options.text: It pays people to bear the swings.
options.feedback: Right. Investors want higher returns for taking more risk, so riskier things tend to pay more.

transfer.stem: Two firms ask Ramesh, a retired teacher in Mysuru, to buy their bonds. One is a steady power company; the other is a new startup. Which likely offers the higher interest?
transfer.hint: Which firm is the bigger gamble for a lender?

options.text: The startup.
options.feedback: Right. A bond is a loan, and lenders want higher returns for taking more risk, so the startup pays more.

options.text: The power company, as it is bigger.
options.feedback: A big, steady firm is less risky, so lenders accept lower interest from it.

options.text: Both the same, since both are bonds.
options.feedback: Bonds differ in risk, and riskier ones tend to pay more interest.

twist.stem: Ravi kept savings in shares for 25 years for a goal. Now the goal is just a year away. What fits the step?
twist.hint: How much time is left to recover from a drop?

options.text: Keep it in shares, as they did well so far.
options.feedback: Past gains do not stop a fall next year. With little time left, lower risk fits better.

options.text: Shift it toward lower-risk savings.
options.feedback: Right. Money needed soon has little time to recover from a fall, so lower-risk places suit it.

options.text: Add riskier shares.
options.feedback: A late drop could hit just when he needs the money. Near a goal, risk should come down.

transfer.stem: Gayatri's family in Vizag needs money for a flat down payment in four months. Her uncle suggests shares "to grow it a bit." What is the concern?
transfer.hint: Think about what a short wait allows after a drop.

options.text: Shares can dip, but they tend to recover within a few months.
options.feedback: Shares can fall at any time, and four months may not be enough to recover. Money needed soon suits lower risk.

options.text: None; shares grow the most, so they fit.
options.feedback: Shares have earned most over long spans. Four months is too short to wait out a dip.

options.text: A fall could hit right when the money is due.
options.feedback: Right. Money needed soon has no time to wait out a drop, so it suits lower-risk savings.

twist.stem: Zaid holds ten firms in equal amounts. One of them falls 40%. About how much does his whole mix fall from that one drop?
twist.hint: What share of his money sat in that firm?

options.text: About 4%.
options.feedback: Right. That firm held a tenth of his money, so a 40% fall cuts the whole mix by about 4%.

options.text: About 40%.
options.feedback: Only a tenth of his money was in that firm, so the whole mix falls much less.

options.text: About 10%.
options.feedback: The firm was a tenth of the mix, but it fell 40%, not all the way. A tenth of 40% is about 4%.

transfer.stem: Sunil drives for one ride app. Ritu drives for two apps and also tutors in the evenings. If one app cuts its pay, whose income takes the smaller hit?
transfer.hint: How much of each income rests on that one app?

options.text: Sunil's, as one app is simpler.
options.feedback: Simple is not safer here. All of Sunil's income rests on that one app.

options.text: Ritu's.
options.feedback: Right. Her income comes from several sources, so one cut hits just part of it.

options.text: Both the same, as it is one app.
options.feedback: The cut is the same, but Ritu has other income to carry on, so her hit is smaller.

twist.stem: Asha holds four shares, each in a different industry. Is that a real spread?
twist.hint: How many firms does a real spread need?

options.text: Yes; different industries are all that counts.
options.feedback: Different industries help, but the number of firms matters too. Four is too few.

options.text: Yes; four firms is plenty.
options.feedback: Four or five shares are not a real spread. A dozen or more is the aim.

options.text: No; four or five shares is too few.
options.feedback: Right. Four or five shares are not a real spread. A dozen or more, across many industries, is the aim.

transfer.stem: A grocery shop in Nashik stocks 30 brands, all of them biscuits. A jump in sugar prices hits biscuit makers. Is the shop spread out?
transfer.hint: Would one shock hit every brand?

options.text: Not really; its goods share one risk.
options.feedback: Right. Many names in one line still rise and fall together, so one shock hits them all.

options.text: Yes, as 30 brands is a lot.
options.feedback: Many names in one line share the same risk. A spread needs different kinds of goods.

options.text: Yes, as each brand is a different firm.
options.feedback: Different firms in one line still share one risk, like a sugar price jump.

twist.stem: Pranav holds 25 shares across many industries. A friend tells him he cannot lose money now. What is missing?
twist.hint: Which shock touches nearly all firms?

options.text: Nothing; 25 firms make losses impossible.
options.feedback: Many holdings can still fall at the same time, as in a market crash.

options.text: A market-wide fall can still pull most down.
options.feedback: Right. A broad mix cuts risk from one firm, but it cannot stop a fall across the whole market.

options.text: He could lose a little, unless he holds 50 or more firms.
options.feedback: No number of firms removes the risk of a market-wide fall. A mix cuts risk; it does not end it.

transfer.stem: A farmer in Karnataka grows five crops instead of one. Which trouble does the mix help with least?
transfer.hint: Which trouble touches the whole farm?

options.text: A pest that attacks just the tomatoes.
options.feedback: A pest on one crop is one part of the mix. The other crops carry on.

options.text: A price drop for one crop.
options.feedback: A drop for one crop is softened by the others. That is the kind of trouble a mix helps with.

options.text: A drought that hits all his fields.
options.feedback: Right. A mix guards against trouble in one part, but a shock to everything hits all the crops.

twist.stem: Raj owns 300 of Firm A's 3,000 shares. Sita owns 100 of Firm B's 500 shares. Who owns the bigger slice of their firm?
twist.hint: Compare each count with its firm's total.

options.text: Sita, with a fifth.
options.feedback: Right. 100 of 500 is a fifth, while 300 of 3,000 is a tenth.

options.text: Raj.
options.feedback: Your slice depends on your shares out of all the shares. Raj's 300 is a tenth of his firm.

options.text: The same.
options.feedback: Their slices differ. Sita holds a fifth of her firm and Raj a tenth of his.

transfer.stem: Three college friends in Pune split their food truck into 90 equal shares, 30 each. They then sell 30 new shares to an investor. What is each friend's slice now?
transfer.hint: Count all the shares after the sale.

options.text: A third, as each still holds 30.
options.feedback: Their count stayed the same, but the total grew. Your slice is your shares out of all shares.

options.text: A quarter.
options.feedback: Right. There are now 120 shares, and each friend holds 30, so each owns a quarter.

options.text: A sixth.
options.feedback: Check the total: 90 plus 30 is 120 shares. Thirty of 120 is a quarter.

twist.stem: Meenal owns a handful of shares in a big bank. A friend says only big owners get to vote. Is that right?
twist.hint: What comes with being a part owner?

options.text: Yes; small owners have no say at the meeting.
options.feedback: Small owners can vote too. Owning shares gives a vote at the general meeting.

options.text: Yes, unless she works at the bank.
options.feedback: Working there does not give a vote. Owning shares does.

options.text: No; a few shares still carry a vote.
options.feedback: Right. Owners of shares can vote on big decisions at the firm's general meeting, whatever their size.

transfer.stem: At a firm's general meeting, owners vote on a plan to open a new factory. Which person there is voting as an owner?
transfer.hint: Who owns a piece of the firm?

options.text: Farah, who holds a few of its shares.
options.feedback: Right. Holding shares makes her a part owner, so she can vote at the general meeting.

options.text: Arun, a top salesman with no shares.
options.feedback: Working for the firm does not make him an owner. Voting comes with holding shares.

options.text: Kamal, a supplier who sells it steel.
options.feedback: Selling to the firm gives no ownership or vote. Holding shares does.

twist.stem: A young firm pays no dividend and puts all its profit back into growth. Why might its owners still be pleased?
twist.hint: What else can owners gain besides a payout?

options.text: They may get the skipped dividend later, as a debt owed to them.
options.feedback: A dividend is never owed. The firm decides if and when to pay.

options.text: The firm, and so their slice, may be worth more.
options.feedback: Right. Owners can also benefit if the company grows, even without a payout.

options.text: They get a fixed payment, like on a loan.
options.feedback: A share is ownership, not a loan, so there is no fixed payment.

transfer.stem: Seema rents out her flat in Thane and gets the same rent each month. She buys shares, expecting the dividend to work the same way. What is different?
transfer.hint: Who makes the call?

options.text: Dividends are paid each week.
options.feedback: There is no set weekly payout. The firm decides if and when it pays.

options.text: None; a dividend is a fixed rent too.
options.feedback: A dividend is not fixed or owed. The company can pay less, or nothing.

options.text: The firm decides if it pays at all.
options.feedback: Right. A dividend may come, but the company decides if, when and how much, so it is not like set rent.

twist.stem: Which of these is a fair use of an emergency fund?
twist.hint: Which cost came without warning?

options.text: A repair after a bike crash.
options.feedback: Right. An emergency fund is cash kept for a sudden need, like an unplanned repair.

options.text: A planned trip with friends to Goa.
options.feedback: A planned trip is known in advance, so it comes from the budget, not the fund.

options.text: Diwali gifts, which come each year.
options.feedback: Diwali comes each year, so gifts are known costs, not an emergency.

transfer.stem: Nikita's firm in Bengaluru shuts down with no warning, and her pay stops. What role fits her emergency fund?
transfer.hint: Is this a sudden need?

options.text: Buying a new phone to cheer herself up.
options.feedback: A treat is not a sudden need. The fund is for shocks like her lost salary.

options.text: Covering living costs while she finds work.
options.feedback: Right. A sudden loss of income is the kind of need an emergency fund is for.

options.text: Staying untouched, as it is for hospital bills.
options.feedback: Hospital bills are one example, not the only one. A sudden job loss is also an emergency.

twist.stem: Arpita spends ₹12,000 a month and has a steady government job. What is the least her emergency fund should hold?
twist.hint: Count the months for a steady job.

options.feedback: One month is too thin. The aim is at least three months of living costs.
Six months is for less secure work. With a steady job, three months is the floor.
Right. With steady work, the aim is at least three months of costs: three times ₹12,000.

transfer.stem: Salim earns from photo shoots in Jaipur, with busy months and empty ones. His costs are ₹20,000 a month. What fund target fits?
transfer.hint: How steady is his income?

options.text: Six months or more, about ₹1,20,000.
options.feedback: Right. With less secure income, the aim is six months or more of living costs.

options.text: Three months, about ₹60,000, like anyone.
options.feedback: Three months is the floor for steady jobs. Shaky income calls for six months or more.

options.text: One month is enough.
options.feedback: A month is too thin, and shoots may not come when needed. Shaky income calls for more.

twist.stem: Tushar keeps his emergency fund in a long fixed deposit that pays more but takes time to break. What is the trade-off?
twist.hint: Think about speed when a bill arrives.

options.text: None; a deposit is cash, so it is ideal.
options.feedback: Cash that takes time to free up is not easy to reach. The fund should be ready at once.

options.text: A better return, but slower to reach.
options.feedback: Right. The fund works best in an easy-to-reach savings account, so a shock can be met at once.

options.text: None, as it cannot lose.
options.feedback: Reach matters most. An emergency may not wait while the deposit is broken.

transfer.stem: Rekha keeps her emergency cash in the same account she uses for daily UPI spending. In three months it shrinks to half, with no emergency. What went wrong?
transfer.hint: Think about money that sits right beside what you spend.

options.text: It should have been kept in gold.
options.feedback: Gold is slow to sell. A separate, easy-to-reach savings account fits better.

options.text: UPI payments carry high fees.
options.feedback: Fees were not the issue. Her fund sat with daily money, so it got spent.

options.text: It mixed with her daily spending.
options.feedback: Right. Kept apart, the fund stays whole. Mixed in, it slowly gets spent on daily things.

twist.stem: Divya says her EMI is all interest, so her loan never shrinks. What is wrong?
twist.hint: What else does each payment cover?

options.text: Part of each EMI also cuts the loan.
options.feedback: Right. An EMI pays that month's interest and part of the loan sum, so the loan shrinks.

options.text: It is all loan.
options.feedback: That is the other mix-up. Each EMI pays some interest first, then cuts the loan with the rest.

options.text: She is right.
options.feedback: EMIs pay both interest and part of the loan sum, so the loan does shrink.

transfer.stem: Mohan takes a fixed-rate loan for a tractor in his village near Indore. A friend says his EMI will rise as the years go by. What is right?
transfer.hint: What does a fixed rate do to the payment?

options.text: It rises as the loan ages.
options.feedback: The payment does not climb on a fixed-rate loan. It stays the same each month.

options.text: It stays the same each month.
options.feedback: Right. On a fixed-rate loan, the EMI stays the same each month.

options.text: It drops each month as the loan shrinks.
options.feedback: The mix inside the EMI shifts, but the EMI itself stays the same on a fixed-rate loan.

twist.stem: Anu still owes ₹80,000 at 1% a month. Today she pays ₹40,000 extra off the loan. What is next month's interest?
twist.hint: Work out what she still owes first.

options.text: ₹800, on the old balance.
options.feedback: Interest is worked out on what is still unpaid. After the extra payment, that is ₹40,000.

options.text: ₹1,000, on the first loan.
options.feedback: Interest does not stay on the first amount. It uses the sum still due.
Right. She now owes ₹40,000, and 1% of that is ₹400. Interest uses the sum still due.

transfer.stem: Babu borrowed ₹60,000 from his uncle at 2% a month and has repaid ₹30,000. His uncle still charges 2% on ₹60,000. What is off?
transfer.hint: How much has he paid back?

options.text: Interest should be on the ₹30,000 still owed.
options.feedback: Right. As a loan shrinks, later interest uses the sum still due, which is ₹30,000.

options.text: Interest stays on the first sum, so it is fair.
options.feedback: Interest is worked out on the loan still unpaid, not the first amount.

options.text: He should now pay 4% a month instead.
options.feedback: The rate does not change. What changes is the sum the rate is worked on.

twist.stem: Vinita can shrink her EMI by stretching her loan from 3 years to 6, at the same rate. What else changes?
twist.hint: How long do the payments run?

options.text: Total interest goes down too.
options.feedback: A smaller EMI does not mean a cheaper loan. Paying for longer adds interest.

options.text: Total interest goes up.
options.feedback: Right. A longer term makes each EMI smaller but means paying interest for longer.

options.text: The rate goes up.
options.feedback: The rate stays the same here. Total interest rises because it runs for more months.

transfer.stem: A phone shop offers Neel a choice: repay ₹40,000 over 12 months or 24, at the same rate. He picks 24 "to save money." What is the catch?
transfer.hint: Count how many months the charges run.

options.text: No catch; smaller payments mean a cheaper loan.
options.feedback: A longer term can lower each payment but raise total interest.

options.text: The rate goes up with the longer plan.
options.feedback: The rate is the same in both plans. The longer one costs more because interest runs longer.

options.text: He pays interest for longer.
options.feedback: Right. A longer term lowers each payment but means paying more interest in total.

twist.stem: One firm makes up 10% of an index. In a fund that follows that index, about what share of the money goes into that firm?
twist.hint: Think about the mix, not just the names.

options.text: About 10%.
options.feedback: Right. An index fund holds the shares in the same proportions as its index.

options.text: About an equal share, like each other firm.
options.feedback: The fund copies the index's mix, not equal slices. A 10% weight in the index means about 10% in the fund.

options.text: Whatever the fund manager thinks is best.
options.feedback: No one picks in an index fund. The index list and its mix decide the holdings.

transfer.stem: Tarun, a shop owner in Kanpur, hears that a firm outside the Nifty 50 jumped sharply this week. Will his Nifty 50 index fund buy it?
transfer.hint: What decides the fund's contents?

options.text: Yes; managers grab the week's winners.
options.feedback: An index fund does not rely on a manager to pick. It follows the list.

options.text: No; it holds what is on the list.
options.feedback: Right. An index fund holds the shares in its index, so a firm off the list is not bought.

options.text: Yes, once the jump is big enough.
options.feedback: A price jump does not put a firm in the fund. Only joining the index does.

twist.stem: Prakash picks an active large-cap fund because its manager is called an expert. Over ten years in India, what has been the more common result for such funds?
twist.hint: Recall how most active large-cap funds did over ten years.

options.text: Beating it.
options.feedback: Most did worse than their index over ten years. A good name does not change that.

options.text: Matching it.
options.feedback: Active funds do not try to match the index. Over ten years, most did worse.

options.text: Doing worse than their index.
options.feedback: Right. Over ten years, most active large-cap funds in India did worse than their index.

transfer.stem: Leena's parents hold ₹1,00,000 in each of two Nifty funds. One charges 0.1% a year and the other 1%. About how much more does the costlier fund take each year?
transfer.hint: Work out each yearly fee in rupees.

options.text: About ₹900.
options.feedback: Right. 1% of ₹1,00,000 is ₹1,000, and 0.1% is ₹100, so the gap is about ₹900 a year.

options.text: About ₹100.
options.feedback: ₹100 is the cheaper fund's fee. The costlier one takes ₹1,000, so the gap is ₹900.

options.text: About ₹1,000.
options.feedback: ₹1,000 is the costlier fund's whole fee. Subtract the cheaper ₹100 to get the gap.

twist.stem: An index rises 12% this year. Fund A returns 11.9% and Fund B returns 10.5%. Both track that index. Which has the larger tracking error?
twist.hint: Which one sits further from the index?

options.text: Fund A.
options.feedback: Fund A trails the index by only 0.1 points. Fund B's gap is far bigger.

options.text: Fund B.
options.feedback: Right. Fund B trails by 1.5 points and Fund A by 0.1, so B has the larger gap.

options.text: Neither, since both rose.
options.feedback: Rising is not the test. Tracking error is the gap between a fund and its index.

transfer.stem: Komal checks her index fund's yearly statement. It is 0.3% behind its index. Her friend says the fund must be badly run. What is a fairer view?
transfer.hint: What leaves a gap even in a well-run fund?

options.text: It should match the index to the paisa.
options.feedback: Fees and running costs leave a small gap, so an exact match is not expected.

options.text: It shows the manager made bad picks.
options.feedback: An index fund does not pick. A small gap comes from costs, not choices.

options.text: Costs cause a small, normal gap.
options.feedback: Right. Expenses and running costs leave a small gap called tracking error.

twist.stem: A message link opens a UPI screen that reads: "Enter PIN to receive your ₹2,000 prize." What does entering the PIN do?
twist.hint: Think about which way the rupees travel.

options.text: It sends ₹2,000 out of your account.
options.feedback: Right. Your PIN approves money going out. Getting money never needs a PIN.

options.text: It accepts the prize into your account.
options.feedback: Receiving money needs no PIN. A screen that asks for one to pay you is a trick.

options.text: It just checks who you are.
options.feedback: The PIN is not an ID check here. Entering it approves a payment out.

transfer.stem: Shabnam, a home tutor, is owed ₹1,200 by a parent. The parent asks her to scan a QR code to "receive" the fee. What should she know?
transfer.hint: Which way do the rupees travel when she pays?

options.text: Scanning is how tutors usually get paid.
options.feedback: Tutors get paid without scanning anything. A scan and PIN make a payment.

options.text: Getting paid needs no scan.
options.feedback: Right. Getting money never needs a QR scan or a PIN, so this request is a warning sign.

options.text: QR codes work both ways, so it is safe.
options.feedback: A QR scan with a PIN sends money. Getting paid needs neither.

twist.stem: Your cousin, who works at a bank, asks for your OTP to speed up your loan form. What fits the rule?
twist.hint: Does the rule have any gaps?

options.text: Share it, since he is family and bank staff.
options.feedback: Being family or bank staff makes no difference. No one needs your OTP.

options.text: Share it if he asks in person, not by phone.
options.feedback: How he asks does not matter. Whoever has the OTP can approve actions on your account.

options.text: Keep it to yourself.
options.feedback: Right. Never share your OTP or PIN with anyone, not even bank staff or family.

transfer.stem: While job hunting, Pranali gets a call from a "recruiter" who asks for the OTP just sent to her phone to verify her profile. What fits the rule?
transfer.hint: What can someone do with that code?

options.text: Refuse; whoever has it can approve actions.
options.feedback: Right. An OTP approves actions on your account, so never share it with anyone.

options.text: Share it, since a real job site may need to check her number.
options.feedback: A real check never needs your OTP. Whoever has it can move money or change your account.

options.text: Share half of it to be careful.
options.feedback: There is no safe part to share. Keep the whole OTP to yourself.

twist.stem: Sunaina was tricked out of money. She has told her bank and blocked UPI. What is her next step?
twist.hint: Where can fraud be reported?

options.text: Wait a week to see if the money comes back.
options.feedback: Waiting loses time. After the bank, report it on 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in.

options.text: Report it on 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in.
options.feedback: Right. Money taken by fraud can be reported on the 1930 helpline or at cybercrime.gov.in.

options.text: Post the scammer's number online first.
options.feedback: Posting online is not a report. Use the 1930 helpline or cybercrime.gov.in.

transfer.stem: Your grandfather in Kochi says a stranger took money from his account two days ago. He wants to wait till Monday to visit his branch. What is best?
transfer.hint: Does speed matter here?

options.text: Wait for Monday, as the branch knows him.
options.feedback: Waiting gives a scammer time. Tell the bank at once and block debits.

options.text: Let it go.
options.feedback: Acting fast can stop more money leaving, and the fraud can be reported on 1930.

options.text: Call the bank now and block debits.
options.feedback: Right. Tell the bank at once and block debits, as speed can stop more money leaving.
